98.3% of all subsale transactions made money. Here’s what we learnt from the other 1.7% that did not.
article:
Most homes bought at a new launch and subsold before the project receives its certificate of statutory completion (CSC) change hands at a profit.

Of over 5,000 subsale transactions across the Core Central Region (CCR), Rest of Central Region (RCR) and Outside Central Region (OCR) between January 2021 and August 2026, 98.3% were subsold above their original purchase price after accounting for seller’s stamp duty (SSD). The finding is based on an EdgeProp Singapore analysis of URA Realis data.

That said, 76 transactions, or 1.5%, recorded a loss. The losses are concentrated in two projects and occur almost entirely among the smallest unit types. Most were also subsold in 2025.

A further nine were subsold at exactly the original purchase price, but likely lost money in practice once buyer’s stamp duty, commission and other costs are factored in. No SSD was deducted from this price, since none was payable on these breakeven transactions.

A subsale is the sale of a unit before the development receives its CSC, according to URA. In EdgeProp Singapore’s analysis, each subsale was matched to the original new sale of the same unit. Profit and loss are stated after accounting for SSD, but before buyer’s stamp duty on the original purchase, additional buyer’s stamp duty, commission and other costs. Units bought from the developer but not subsold in the period fall outside the analysis.

Losses most common in CCR

Loss-making subsales were most common in the CCR, where 7.1% of subsale transactions translated to losses. The RCR followed at 1.9%, and the OCR at 0.7% (see Table 1).

The largest single loss also came from the CCR. A 2,411 sq ft unit at The Avenir , a freehold condo in River Valley, was subsold for $6.9 million in July 2025. This was about $1.1 million or 13% below its original purchase price.

Two RCR projects account for a fifth of all losses

One Pearl Bank and Normanton Park , both in the RCR, recorded eight loss-making subsales each, or 16 of the 76 losses islandwide.

These are the only projects with more than three loss-making subsales each. The remaining 47 projects recorded three or fewer loss-making subsales each. Of these, 12 recorded more than one loss-making subsale (see Table 2).

One Pearl Bank: eight losses from 57 subsales

One Pearl Bank is a 774-unit residential development in the Outram Planning Area, on a 99-year lease from 2019. It occupies the site of the former Pearl Bank Apartments, sold en bloc in 2018.

Eight of One Pearl Bank’s 57 subsales, or 14%, recorded a loss. The largest of these involved a 527 sq ft unit, held for 5.8 years before it changed hands for $1.13 million in May 2025. This was $198,000, or 15%, below the original purchase price.

Normanton Park: eight losses from 207 subsales

A similar pattern can be seen at Normanton Park, a residential development in the Queenstown Planning Area. The project comprises 1,840 apartments and 22 landed homes on a 99-year leasehold from 2019. It sits on the site of a former Housing and Urban Development Co estate of the same name, sold en bloc in 2017.

Eight of Normanton Park’s 207 subsales, or 4%, recorded a loss. The largest of these involved a 527 sq ft unit, held for 3.7 years before it changed hands for $950,000 in November 2025. This was $83,000, or 8%, below the original purchase price. Seven of the eight loss-making units are under 600 sq ft.

What the losses across two projects tell us

Losses concentrated in smallest units

Eight of One Pearl Bank’s 16 small-unit subsales were loss-making, while none of the 41 larger-unit subsales made a loss.

Units under 600 sq ft made up 15% of Normanton Park’s subsales but accounted for seven of the eight losses. This segment recorded a loss rate of about 23%, against less than 1% for larger units (see Table 3).

Small units also posted lower returns than larger units. The median return on units under 600 sq ft was –0.4% at One Pearl Bank and 7.6% at Normanton Park, against 9.0% and 16.3%, respectively, for larger units.

Two factors may explain this. Smaller units tend to command a higher psf. Fixed elements of a home, such as the kitchen, bathroom and entrance, cost roughly the same regardless of unit size, so that cost is spread across a smaller floor area.

Beyond unit size, smaller, lower-quantum units tend to attract a narrower buyer base skewed towards investors rather than families. This narrower pool means fewer exit buyers, which can translate into slower price growth or even loss-making transactions.

One Pearl Bank small units were subsold below their launch price

The average new sale price for units under 600 sq ft at One Pearl Bank rose 16%, from $2,386 psf in 2019 to $2,774 psf in 2022 (see Chart 1). By 2025, the median subsale price for these units was $2,346 psf, below the 2019 launch average.

Normanton Park buyers who entered after the launch year fared worse

Normanton Park sold most of its apartments in 2021, the launch year, and the remainder in 2022. Among units later subsold, those purchased in 2022 made up about 14% of the sample but accounted for half of the project’s losses.

Median return for units bought in 2022 was lower, at 12.5% against 16.3% for units bought in the launch year. The new price for these units was also about 4% higher in 2022 than in 2021.

Most losses clustered in late 2025

Of the 16 loss-making subsales across the two projects, 13 fell in 2025, seven of them in November and December alone.

Holding periods within that group ranged from 3.1 to 6.4 years, suggesting the clustering was not driven by a single buying cohort.

The clustering coincides with lower subsale prices for small units at bothprojects. At One Pearl Bank, the median subsale price of units under 600 sq ft fell from $2,625 psf in 2023 to $2,346 in 2025. Notably, six of the project’s eight losses were sold in 2025.

At Normanton Park, the median subsale price for the same size band fell from $2,051 psf in 2024 to $1,886 psf in 2025 (see Table 4).

A potential reason for the lower prices could be the deluge of new launches and developer sales.

Over 4,000 new residential units launched in 3Q2025 alone, giving buyers in the small-unit, lower-quantum segment a much wider pool of alternatives. New home sales also increased by nearly threefold to 3,288 units in the same quarter, compared to 2Q2025, suggesting more buyer demand towards new launches instead of older subsale units.

Overall, profits outweigh losses in scale and count

SSD-adjusted profits across the 4,991 profitable subsales totalled $1.32 billion, 176 times the $7.5 million lost across all loss-making transactions. Average gains and losses came to $265,000 and $99,000 respectively. Meanwhile, the median profit reached 18.8%.

Losses were shallow too. The median loss stood at 4.3%, with 42 of the 76 losses within 5% of the purchase price.

The three largest gains alone, all at Boulevard 88 and led by a $3.87 million profit, exceeded the $7.5 million lost across all 76 loss-making transactions.

title: Singapore property market sentiment rebounds in 2Q2026 on stronger economic growth: NUS
article:
Industry sentiment in Singapore’s real estate market rebounded in 2Q2026, supported by stronger-than-expected economic growth in the first half of the year, according to the latest Real Estate Sentiment Index (Resi) published by the National University of Singapore (NUS).

The Composite Sentiment Index rose to 5.6 in 2Q2026, from 4.9 in the preceding quarter. The Current Sentiment Index similarly increased to 5.6 from 4.9, while the Future Sentiment Index climbed to 5.5 from 5.0.

The Current Sentiment Index tracks changes over the past six months, while the Future Sentiment Index measures expectations for the next six months. Both are aggregated to derive the Composite Sentiment Index, which indicates overall market sentiment.

The improvement marks a turnaround from 1Q2026, when all three indices had weakened amid heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.

Prof Qian Wenlan, director of NUS Institute of Real Estate and Urban Studies (Ireus), attributed the improvement to a more sanguine economic outlook following Singapore’s stronger-than-expected performance in 1H2026.

She noted that commercial space, including offices, business parks and industrial and logistics properties, contributed significantly to the rally.

Produced by NUS’ Department of Real Estate and Ireus, the Resi tracks perceptions and expectations of the real estate market through quarterly surveys of senior executives in Singapore real estate firms.

Office sentiment hits multi-year high

Among the property sectors surveyed, offices recorded the strongest improvement. The sector’s current net balance surged 36 percentage points q-o-q to 36% in 2Q2026, from 0% in the preceding quarter, reaching its highest level in several years. Its future net balance stood at 27%.

One survey respondent cited a limited supply of new offices and a better economic outlook.

Sentiment towards other commercial and industrial sectors also brightened. The current net balance for business parks and hi-tech space rose to 5%, from –25% in 1Q2026, while industrial and logistics properties improved to +9%, from –5%.

However, retail sentiment remained subdued. Prime retail recorded a current net balance of –23%, while suburban retail stood at –18%.

Suburban residential sentiment weakens

In contrast to the broader rebound, sentiment towards suburban residential property weakened sharply.

Its current net balance fell to –14% in 2Q2026, from 15% in the previous quarter, marking its first negative reading in over a year. Its future net balance also declined from 15% to –5%.

Qian attributed the decline to a combination of affordability constraints, supply pressures and policy changes.

“Mass-market suburban housing is predominantly driven by domestic owner-occupiers and HDB upgraders,” she said.

With suburban new launch prices reaching new highs, affordability has become a greater constraint and buyer resistance appears to have emerged, she added.

Qian also pointed to the recent increase in income ceilings for Build-To-Order flats and executive condos , to $16,000 and $18,000 respectively. The changes widen the pool of households eligible for subsidised housing and could reduce the urgency among some buyers to enter the suburban private housing market, she says.

Prime residential property fared better in terms of current sentiment, with its current net balance rising to 9% from 5% in 1Q2026. However, its future net balance stood at –14%.

Among developers surveyed, 70% expect the number of new residential launches over the next six months to remain broadly unchanged, up from 60% in the previous quarter.

Another 20% expect a moderately higher number of launches, while 10% anticipate a moderately lower number.

Half of the developers expect prices at new residential launches to remain unchanged over the next six months. Meanwhile, 30% expect moderately higher prices and 20% anticipate moderately lower prices.

Developers remain cautious on outlook

Looking ahead, a slowdown in the global economy and rising inflation and interest rates were the most commonly cited risks to property market sentiment, each flagged by 81.8% of respondents.

Job losses and a decline in the domestic economy were cited by 59.1% of respondents, while 45.5% highlighted rising construction costs.

Concerns over an excessive supply of new property launches also increased, with 18.2% of respondents identifying it as a risk, compared with 5% in 1Q2026. Meanwhile, concerns over further government demand-side cooling measures fell to 13.6%, from 40% in the previous quarter.

Development costs remain a key concern among developers. Some 90% expressed concern over building material costs, while 80% cited financing and labour costs. Another 70% were concerned about land costs.

title: Seller at Ardmore Park in prime District 10 scores $7.6 mil in profit
article:
The most profitable condo resale transaction for the period of Sept 8 to 15 came from Ardmore Park , a freehold development in District 10.

A 2,885 sq ft four-bedder on the ninth floor fetched $12.55 million ($4,350 psf) on Sept 8. The owner netted a profit of $7.6 million (153.6%), having purchased the unit for $4.95 million ($1,716 psf) in August 1996. On an annualised basis, it works out to 3.1% over 30 years.

This ranks as Ardmore Park’s fifth most profitable transaction to date. The biggest windfall came from a January 2025 deal, when another four-bedroom unit on the seventh floor changed hands for $13.2 million. The seller raked in $8.54 million in profit, having bought it for $4.66 million in May 2002.

Completed in 2001, the 330-unit Ardmore Park is located in the Ardmore -Draycott residential enclave. The freehold condo consists mainly of four-bedroom units measuring 2,885 sq ft, along with six duplex penthouses, each spanning 8,740 sq ft.

Data compiled by EdgeProp Singapore shows that the development recorded four other resale deals this year, all of them profitable. These units were priced from $11.05 million to $12.68 million, with gains ranging from $3.5 million to $7.61 million.

Coming in second on the gains’ table during the week was a three-storey unit at freehold project Glentrees in District 10.

On Sept 9, the 3,671 sq ft, four-bedroom unit changed hands for $5.6 million ($1,526 psf), scoring a profit of $3.91 million. The owner had originally purchased it from the developer for around $1.69 million ($460 psf) in August 2004. That translates to an annualised gain of 5.6% across slightly over 22 years.

This is also Glentree’s most profitable deal thus far, surpassing the previous record set in February 2024. In that transaction, the seller reaped a profit of $2.9 million from the sale of another four-bedder for $4.4 million. It was initially bought for $1.5 million in August 2004.

Located on Mount Sinai Lane, Glentrees is a 999-year leasehold development completed in 2005.

Its eight five-storey blocks house a total of 176 units. They range from two- to four-bedders measuring 1,346 to 1,884 sq ft.

The development also has top-floor loft units ranging from 1,991 to 2,691 sq ft, as well as Garden Terraces with two- and three-storey layouts spanning 2,626 to 3,671 sq ft.

Meanwhile, the steepest loss among this week’s most unprofitable condo resale deals came from District 1 condo Marina Bay Suites .

On the 50th floor, a 2,056 sq ft four-bedder recorded a $1.73 million loss when it fetched $4.2 million ($2,043 psf) on Sept 8. The seller previously bought the unit for $5.93 million ($2,886 psf) in May 2010, resulting in an annualised loss of 2.1% over more than 16 years.

Despite the seven-figure loss, that was not the most unprofitable deal at Marina Bay Suites. The record was a $3.25 million loss from the resale of a larger four-bedroom unit. It was purchased for $8.25 million in 2013, and changed hands for $5 million in August 2022.

Marina Bay Suites is a 221-unit development located on Central Boulevard in the Marina Bay financial district.

Completed in 2013, the 99-year leasehold condo is part of the Marina Bay Financial Centre mixed-use complex. It has three- and four-bedders measuring between 1,572 and 2,691 sq ft.

title: Freehold condo Latitude notches new price high of $2,993 psf
article:
Among private non-landed residential developments that set fresh psf-price peaks during the week of Sept 8 to 15, Latitude topped the list at $2,993 psf.

The new record at the freehold development occurred with the sale of a 2,766 sq ft four-bedder on the 17th floor for $8.28 million on Sept 11.

That is the second time a unit at Latitude has transacted above the $2,900 psf threshold. It inches past the project’s former price high of $2,932 psf, established with the sale of a 1,927 sq ft, three-bedroom unit for $5.65 million in July 2023.

Latitude is a 127-unit condo on Jalan Mutiara in River Valley. It comprises two- to four-bedroom units ranging from 1,324 to 2,928 sq ft, as well as a 5,317 sq ft penthouse and a 5,113 sq ft duplex penthouse.

It is within a 10-minute walk of dining and retail amenities at Great World.

The highest quantum ever recorded at the development was for the 5,113 sq ft duplex penthouse that fetched $12.5 million in January 2013.

Clinching second place for the week was a transaction at The Imperial in prime District 9. On Sept 10, a 1,905 sq ft three-bedder on the ninth floor fetched $5.32 million, scoring a new record of $2,793 psf.

It surpasses the project’s previous high of $2,659 psf. That was set on March 25, when a smaller three-bedroom unit changed hands for $3.75 million.

Located along Jalan Rumbia near Fort Canning Park, The Imperial is a freehold condo completed in 2006. It comprises 187 units across five residential blocks, with a mix of two- to four-bedders of 980 to 3,918 sq ft.

Based on caveats compiled by EdgeProp Singapore , The Imperial has an average resale price of $2,566 psf across transactions in the past 12 months. This is higher than the averages at nearby freehold developments within a 1km radius, including Oxley Edge and Belle Vue Residences , which stand at $1,529 psf and $2,150 psf, respectively.

A District 15 project, Moda , also hit a new psf-price peak during the week. The freehold boutique project set a fresh record of $2,226 psf with the sale of a 980 sq ft, two-bedroom apartment for $2.18 million on Sept 9.

It edges out Moda’s previous price high of $2,195, which involved the sale of a similarly sized apartment for  $2.15 million in July last year.

Completed in 2014, Moda is located along East Coast Road in Marine Parade. The development comprises 56 apartments, most of which are two-bedders ranging from 646 to 980 sq ft. There are also five three-bedroom apartments measuring between 1,615 and 1,894 sq ft.

The Sept 9 deal marks Moda’s first caveated transaction since 2025. Caveats show only two transactions at the development last year: a 764 sq ft two-bedder that was sold for $1.56 million ($2,041 psf), and a 980 sq ft apartment that changed hands for $2.15 million ($2,195 psf).

No psf-price lows were recorded for the week.

title: The silent cost of not having a property succession plan
article:
For most families in Singapore, the family home is the single largest asset they will ever own and, very often, the single largest asset they will ever pass on. It represents decades of mortgage payments, decisions and sacrifice. Yet when I ask clients directly what the plan is for that property once they are no longer around, the majority have never seriously thought about it.

The default answer almost everyone reaches for is some version of: pay down the mortgage, let the property appreciate and eventually split it between the kids or sell it and split the proceeds. Or rightsize and channel the funds into their retirement. It sounds simple. In practice, it rarely is.

Here is what that default plan can actually look like once it meets a real family.

Two daughters, one house

Take a couple I will call the Teos. They bought a condo decades ago and paid it off the way most people do: working hard, staying disciplined and becoming mortgage-free by the time they retired. It is worth about $2 million today. They have two daughters. The elder married some years ago and lives with her husband in their own place. The younger never left and, by the time the parents pass away, she is still the one living in the family home, with nowhere else lined up.

The Teos’ plan for the property, to the extent they had one, was simple and fair: split the house between both daughters.

Except a house does not actually split in half. On paper, each daughter now owns half of a $2 million property. In practice, the younger daughter is living in the whole of it and the elder daughter, who has her own mortgage to pay and no use for half a home she does not live in, starts to feel she has come out of this worse off.

She did not inherit an equal share; she inherited a stake in a property she cannot use unless her sister sells it or pays her something for it. So she asks for rent. Her younger sister, who never asked to inherit half a house she was already living in, does not see why she should suddenly start paying rent on a home that is half hers anyway.

Neither of them is being unreasonable. They have inherited a disagreement along with the asset, and it is already changing how they speak to each other.

I have sat across the table from enough families to know this is not a rare story and it is not really a story about anyone being greedy either.

It is what happens when a large, illiquid asset gets divided equally on paper between two people whose actual circumstances — where they live, what they need and what they can afford — are not equal at all.

“Split it between the kids” sounds like a plan. It is really just a default scenario, which does not account for who is still living in the house when the time comes.

Why the plan almost never exists

Part of the reason this catches families off-guard is that property planning rarely gets treated as real planning at all. There is a retirement plan, there is an investment portfolio, there is CPF and then there is “the house”, treated as a different category of decision entirely.

Retirement in Singapore is also getting longer, not shorter. People are living well into their 80s and 90s, while property values keep climbing in the background regardless of whether anyone has thought about what happens to that value later.

Left alone long enough, the two habits combine into exactly what happened to the Teos: a valuable asset with no real instructions attached to it beyond “split it equally”.

Property planning is not supposed to be a separate conversation from financial planning. It is supposed to be the same one, and that includes thinking through what happens when more than one person inherits a home that only one of them is actually living in.

One way to build in liquidity

There is more than one way to avoid the position the Teos’ daughters ended up in. Some families simply update their wills earlier and have the harder conversations while everyone is still around to have them.

Others set aside a separate savings or insurance plan over time, entirely without touching the property, specifically so there is cash on hand alongside the house.

And some families use the equity already sitting in the property to build that cash pool, which is worth walking through as one concrete example, not because it is the only answer, but because it shows what planning ahead can actually look like in practice.

Take another couple I will refer to as the Tans, who also have two daughters: one married and living elsewhere, and the other still at home.

Rather than leave the same problem for their daughters to sort out, the Tans decide, 10 years before they are anywhere near “mortgage-free”, to draw a separate loan against the equity they have already built up in their $2 million condo — say, $500,000 — at the kind of interest rate you only get when a bank knows your house is the security.

Because they still have an active income at that point, the bank is willing to lend. Their reasoning is that this window will not stay open forever: borrowing tends to get harder, not easier, as retirement approaches.

The Tans take $300,000 of that amount and invest it steadily over the years that follow. Alongside the investment, they also take out a term insurance plan, sized at around $900,000, that pays out a fixed sum on death no matter how the investment has performed.

It is an added cost on top of the loan and the investment, but it means the family is not relying entirely on markets doing well to have something certain waiting for their daughters.

To be fair to the concern I know some readers will have here: this is not free money, and it is not risk-free either.

Carrying that extra $500,000 for 15 years, on top of their existing mortgage, means the Tans pay real interest on it — in this case, somewhere around $80,000 to $100,000 more over those years than if they had never touched the equity at all.

If their income had dropped during that period, whether from a job loss, illness or early retirement, servicing that extra loan alongside the mortgage would have been considerably harder, in the same way it would be harder for anyone carrying a larger mortgage without a buffer.

And the $300,000 they invested was never guaranteed to grow; it was invested in a diversified way over a long horizon specifically because markets can and do have bad years, sometimes bad decades.

None of this is a promise. It is a deliberate trade they made with their eyes open. It is really the distinction worth sitting with: the Tans are not avoiding risk, and Singapore’s lending rules would not let them overleverage even if they wanted to.

What they are doing is taking a calculated risk, sized to what they can actually afford, and backing it with something — the term insurance — that does not depend on the calculation being right.

With that said, here is the outcome they were aiming for, using a fairly ordinary long-term rate of return. That $300,000, invested for 15 years instead of sitting frozen in the walls of the condo, could potentially grow to somewhere between $715,000 and $820,000.

Subtract the $100,000 in extra interest it cost them to access it early, and the Tans end up with a net gain somewhere between $615,000 and $720,000 — capital that would not have been generated in the same way if they had waited until the mortgage was fully paid before thinking about what else the property could do.

When the Tans eventually pass away, the term insurance pays out its fixed sum straight away; insurance payouts in Singapore typically move faster than the rest of an estate does. The investment they started 15 years earlier is also there, sitting in cash rather than tied up in the property.

Between the two, there is an amount that comes reasonably close to the value of the home itself. That was really the point of setting it up this way: instead of leaving both daughters with a shared claim on one property, the Tans leave one daughter the home she is already living in and the other a cash amount she can use however she wants, without needing to ask her sister to sell, move out or pay rent.

It assumes the investment performed reasonably over that period, which is exactly why the trade-offs are worth being honest about.

The trade-offs, honestly

This is the part that deserves more space than a single disclaimer at the bottom of the page, because an example like the Tans’ looks good only if you focus on the version where things go reasonably well.

Start with income. The Tans’ plan assumed they could keep servicing both the mortgage and the extra loan on an active income for 15 years. If one of them had been retrenched, fallen seriously ill or had to stop working earlier than planned, that assumption would break, and carrying two loans on a reduced income would be harder than carrying one.

This is not a risk unique to borrowing against home equity; anyone with a mortgage faces the same exposure.

But it does mean the decision to draw a second loan should come with a genuine buffer built in from the start: enough savings or insurance coverage to keep servicing the debt through a period without income, not just a plan that works if everything goes as expected.

That buffer needs to cover the insurance premiums too, since those still fall due even if income stops. A family without that buffer, or without the appetite to build one, is better off not taking this route, full stop.

Then there is the investment side. The investment returns in the Tans’ example are assumed to be fairly long-term.

Markets do not move in a straight line. A poorly timed downturn, especially one that lands in the years just before the money is needed, could leave that $300,000 investment worth significantly less than projected and, in a bad enough stretch, less than what was borrowed to fund it.

This is exactly why the money should go into something diversified and appropriate for the time horizon, not a concentrated bet, and why anyone doing this needs to be genuinely comfortable holding through a downturn rather than being forced to sell at the bottom because the loan repayments will not wait.

Interest rates matter too. The Tans borrowed when rates on the additional loan were low relative to history. If rates rise meaningfully during the loan period, the extra interest cost could end up well above the $80,000 used in this example, which narrows the gap between this approach and simply leaving the equity untouched.

And if a weaker investment period lines up with a higher-rate environment at the same time, the numbers can move against you on both sides at once. That combination is the actual worst case worth planning for, not the best case used to illustrate the idea.

None of this means the approach is wrong for every family. It means it is conditional. It depends on having a genuine income buffer, a realistic and diversified investment approach, and an honest look at what happens if rates move against you.

For some households, once you run those numbers, the case still holds up. For others, it does not, and the more conservative path of paying down the mortgage and holding the property outright might be the right one.

That is a decision worth making deliberately, with a proper look at the numbers, rather than defaulting into either option without having thought it through.

The tool matters less than having an answer

For a lot of families, an equity loan will not be the right tool at all, and that is fine.

There are plenty of ways to build in liquidity for the next generation, or for your own later years, without borrowing against the house: a term insurance plan on its own, a separate savings pot built up over time, or simply having the will and the harder conversations sorted out earlier, while everyone is still around to have them.

What the Tans did is one way of solving the problem, not the only way, and it is not for everyone.

If your income is a single, concentrated source with little room for disruption, if you do not have the buffer to absorb a bad few years in the markets or a period without income, or if the idea of any new loan keeps you up at night regardless of the numbers, then borrowing against the house might be the wrong tool for you, and that is a completely reasonable place to land. Peace of mind counts for something too, and it is not a lesser plan.

What matters far more than which tool a family picks is that they pick one at all. The Teos did not do anything reckless. They did not overspend, did not take on debt they could not handle and did not make any obviously bad decision.

They just never got around to asking what would actually happen when their $2 million home is passed to two daughters living very different lives. That is the gap worth closing, not because there is one right answer, but because a family’s biggest asset deserves more than a default option.

The house was never meant to be the whole plan on its own. Whether the answer ends up being a will that spells things out clearly, an insurance policy, a savings pot or something like what the Tans did via an equity release on their property, the point is not which tool a family chooses. It is making sure their biggest asset comes with an actual answer instead of an assumption nobody ever tested.

Disclaimer: This article is for general information only and is not legal, tax or financial advice. It describes possible approaches among several, not a recommendation to borrow or invest. The numbers are simplified examples, not promises of what any loan will cost or any investment will actually return, and the risks discussed, including income loss, rising interest rates and weaker investment returns, are real and should be assessed properly before acting. Please speak to a licensed financial adviser and a lawyer before making any borrowing, investment or estate-planning decisions.

title: Bitcoin bulls eye next leg as US$15 bil options expiry nears
article:
(Sept 24): Traders seeking clues as to whether the Bitcoin rally is sustainable are turning their attention to one of the must-watch events in the derivatives market: the quarterly expiration of roughly US$15 billion in options contracts.

More than a third of all Bitcoin options open interest, or total contracts, on Deribit that is set to expire on Friday is tied to the Sept 25 expiry. The put-to-call ratio — a closely followed measure of options to sell versus ones to buy — stands at 0.70, indicating there are more bets on higher prices. The largest concentrations of call options are clustered at strike prices of US$85,000, US$90,000 and US$100,000.

At around US$84,000, Bitcoin is trading well above the so-called max pain level of US$76,000 — the price at which the largest number of options would expire worthless. That leaves traders watching whether hedging around the large call positions restrains the market before Friday’s settlement.

Options-market positioning often puts a temporary lid on rallies. Dealers are broadly neutral around current prices, but are positioned in a way that can prompt them to sell as Bitcoin rises towards US$90,000 to US$95,000 in order to keep their hedges balanced, potentially dampening gains until the options expire.

“Hedging activity may therefore be dampening rallies until expiry, and momentum could resume once these options expire or are rolled towards the next quarterly expiry,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets, a digital-asset derivatives liquidity provider.

The options-market turning point comes after a powerful recovery in Bitcoin that began in August, when the US Treasury buyback announcement helped drive most risk assets higher. Bitcoin has gained over 30% since.

See also: Bitcoin ETF flows turn positive after US$4.6 bil rebound

The setup follows a record options expiry last week for BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT). Those contracts were heavily tilted towards calls, and Bitcoin’s rally pushed many of them into profit, forcing dealers that had sold the options to buy IBIT shares to hedge their exposure, according to Mauricio Di Bartolomeo, co-founder of crypto lender Ledn.

That buying can filter through to the underlying cryptocurrency as new ETF shares are created, he said. The Deribit expiry on Friday could produce a similar effect if Bitcoin keeps climbing towards areas with heavy call exposure.

“The crypto-native expiration inherits that setup,” Di Bartolomeo said. “If the move continues, the large call blocks at US$85,000 and US$100,000 are where the same dynamic kicks in on the Deribit book.”

See also: Bitcoin retreats from eight-month high after dizzying 13% rally

Some traders are already looking beyond Friday. Jake Ostrovskis, head of over-the-counter trading at Wintermute, said positions are being shifted into later expiries, with many traders choosing Bitcoin calls at US$95,000 to US$100,000 for October and December. Some longer-dated bets stretch as high as US$150,000 for March 2027.

Still, the size of an expiry alone doesn’t dictate where Bitcoin goes next. Oliver Carding, head of marketing at Tesseract Group, said that it isn’t publicly known who holds the short side of the contracts.

“I would treat the expiry as a positioning and roll event rather than something that sets direction,” he said.

title: Japan 10-year yield climbs to 1996 high as global rout deepens
article:
(Sept 24): Japan’s 10-year government bond yield climbed to its highest since 1996, joining a deepening global sell-off as the market reopened after the Silver Week holidays.

The yield rose 10 basis points to 3.075% on Thursday after the three-day break. Yields across the curve also climbed, with the five-year rate rising 9.5 basis points to 2.37%.

The moves followed an intensifying sell-off in Treasuries, where robust US economic data and weak demand at a debt auction pushed yields across much of the curve to their highest levels in almost two decades. Rising oil prices added to inflation concerns and reinforced expectations for further Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes.

Domestic pressures are adding to the sell-off. The Bank of Japan (BOJ) raised its benchmark rate Friday and left the door open to further tightening, though traders were disappointed by the lack of clearer guidance on the pace of future moves. That leaves Japanese yields exposed to both expectations for additional BOJ hikes and the global repricing of longer-term borrowing costs.

The combination of two dissents against last week’s rate increase and the absence of a proposal for a larger 50-basis-point move has also fuelled concern that the BOJ risks falling behind the curve on inflation, according to Katsutoshi Inadome, senior strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. Those worries, alongside rising US yields, are contributing to the selling, he said.

See also: Fed’s Williams says Treasuries clearing moving ahead of schedule

Fiscal concerns are adding pressure further out the curve. The government is said to be considering a new mid-term defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP, in line with Nato and other US allies, adding to scrutiny over Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s spending plans and how additional expenditure would be financed.

title: NSE shares rise in stock market debut after US$2.4 bil IPO
article:
(Sept 24): National Stock Exchange of India Ltd’s shares gained in their debut on the BSE after the company raised US$2.4 billion ($3.07 billion) in one of the biggest initial public offerings (IPOs) in the country’s history.

The stock rose 0.8% to 1,800 rupees in pre-market trading, compared with an IPO price of 1,785 rupees a share. The deal valued the world’s biggest derivatives exchange at 4.4 trillion rupees (US$46 billion or $59 billion).

The debut gives investors access to one of the linchpins of India’s fast-growing capital market. It’s also a chance to weigh in on the debate over NSE’s worth. On the one hand, the company’s long-term growth trajectory drove healthy institutional demand. On the other, and near-term concerns over derivatives volumes, regulatory headwinds and the prospect of additional share supply kept mom-and-pop investors more cautious.

“NSE’s earnings growth slowed in fiscal 2026 and will likely remain under pressure in the near term due to regulatory scrutiny and higher taxes on equity futures and options trading,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Sharnie Wong wrote in a note Wednesday.

The 226 billion-rupee offering, trailing only Hyundai Motor India Ltd’s 279 billion-rupee share sale in 2024 among India IPOs, was subscribed 5.7 times. Large institutional investors were among the biggest bidders, signalling confidence in NSE’s prospects at a valuation that remains elevated compared with some global exchange operators.

Even after the valuation concerns forced the company to dial back both the size and the price of the listing, the IPO valued NSE the world’s eighth-largest listed exchange by market value, compared with London Stock Exchange Group plc’s about US$52.5 billion.

See also: NSE’s US$2.4 bil IPO gets subdued demand from retail crowd

While investors broadly remain positive about NSE’s long-term prospects, the stock’s performance in the months after listing may hinge on how much additional supply comes to market as lock-in periods for existing shareholders expire.

“There’s little doubt that NSE is an attractive stock to own over the long term, but its near-term performance will likely depend on how much additional supply hits the market over the next few months as lock-in periods expire for existing shareholders,” said Ambareesh Baliga, an independent market analyst.

NSE’s outlook has come under greater scrutiny after regulators tightened rules aimed at curbing excessive speculation in India’s derivatives market. That’s particularly important for the exchange because transaction fees from options trading accounted for more than 60% of operating revenue in fiscal 2026.

Still, NSE has the potential to grow 15% to 20% annually over the next decade, supported by continued product innovation, longer trading hours, its dominant position in equities and emerging revenue streams from commodities, data and other businesses, according to Raamdeo Agrawal, chairman and co-founder of Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd.

“Regulatory headwinds, however, could temper that growth in the short term,” Agrawal said.

Several large investors, including Life Insurance Corp of India, Norges Bank Investment Management, ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co, Quant Mutual Fund and Mirae Asset Mutual Fund, were among the top bidders in NSE’s main book, people familiar with the matter have said.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management, HSBC, Fidelity, Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Eastspring were among the major investors that participated in the anchor book.

Thursday’s listing will cap NSE’s long road to the public markets after its first attempt to go public in 2016 was held up by regulatory and governance issues.

title: Mining giant Rio Tinto plans to expand metals trading business
article:
(Sept 24): Rio Tinto Group plans to expand its marketing operations to trade more metal from other producers as well as derivatives, according to people familiar with its strategy, as part of a drive by its new leader to make the business more agile.

Rio is the world’s second-biggest miner, with operations spanning from iron ore in Western Australia to copper in Mongolia and aluminum in North America. However, historically it has not had a vast trading operation and hasn’t been as successful as some of its peers in extracting maximum value from all parts of its business, something that chairman Dominic Barton and chief executive officer Simon Trott are keen to address.

Rio’s shortcomings were highlighted during two rounds of talks over the past two years to buy Glencore Plc, a mining rival with sprawling trading operations that span energy, metals and power markets. Glencore’s deep-rooted trading networks and commercial acumen were a key attraction for Rio — along with a lucrative copper portfolio. Those discussions were later dropped.

Rio is not aiming to replicate the sector’s standalone trading giants, the people said, asking not to be identified as discussions are ongoing — but it wants to see a step change in the current business, headed by chief commercial officer Bold Baatar.

It will, for example, build out third-party trading — normally the preserve of specialist traders who tend to buy commodities rather than digging them up — marking a significant break from its current model of marketing primarily its own products. Still, Rio sees the shift as a means of squeezing more profit from its assets, rather than as an effort to build a standalone trading business, the people said.

Areas of focus include the alumina market, where it is oversupplied in some geographies and light in others. Rio is also looking at trading opportunities in the North American copper market, where it has spare smelting capacity at its Kennecott operations. The company could add copper cathode and related products like sulfuric acid.

See also: Carney tells NYT he looked at ‘extreme tail risk’ of US invasion

The company is also willing to start using financial derivatives to hedge against its positions and exposures, the people said, rather than taking directional bets on commodity prices.

“Marketing equity tonnes from our own operations to meet the needs of customers and partners remains the foundation of Rio Tinto’s business.” Rio said in a statement. “Alongside this, we are continuing to grow our capability to buy and sell products on behalf of third parties.”

“We see this as an opportunity to deliver added value through maximising infrastructure utilisation, optimising the placement of our own production and offering increased optionality for customers.”

See also: Radiant World sent Mizuho fake Glencore email, court filing says

The company declined to comment further on its plans.

Rio centralised its commercial operations into a marketing hub in Singapore in 2018 — under Trott, who was then chief commercial officer — in attempt to catch up with rival miners BHP Group and Anglo American Plc who had more established marketing arms. Yet those attempts mostly stalled during the pandemic. Anglo reversed course further from 2024, as it fought off a takeover bid.

Under Trott, who became CEO last year, Rio has laid out plans to simplify the business, sell assets and cut costs. Yet it also sought to drive more profit from its operations. The company is already in talks with oil-trading giant Vitol Group about setting up a freight and logistics joint venture, Bloomberg reported in June.

Rio’s commercial team currently has about 20 traders with plans to add another handful, the people said. The financial contribution of the unit will also not be disclosed, but will be measured internally.

title: Hong Kong seeks up to US$2.6 bil in record digital bond sale — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 24): Hong Kong is seeking to raise HK$15 billion to HK$20 billion (US$1.9 billion to US$2.6 billion or $2.45 billion to $3.26 billion) through a multi-currency digital green bond offering that would be the world’s largest of its kind, according to people familiar with the matter, as the city pushes to become a fixed-income hub.

The bonds, denominated in US dollars, Hong Kong dollars, euros and offshore yuan, could be priced as early as Monday, the people said, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. The Hong Kong government has mandated banks to arrange a series of fixed-income meetings this week.

The planned sale would build on Hong Kong’s efforts to expand its market for digital, or tokenised, bonds, which use blockchain technology for issuance, trading and settlement. Chief Executive John Lee has pledged to regularise such issuances to drive innovation and adoption. The transaction would also advance the city’s push to strengthen its fixed-income market through green finance and tokenisation.

A spokesperson for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which acts as the government’s representative in the potential offering, declined to comment.

Hong Kong has been at the forefront of promoting digital bonds, with the government selling roughly HK$10 billion equivalent in such bonds last year. The record was eclipsed in June when Hong Kong Mortgage Corp completed a HK$12 billion-equivalent deal, then the world’s largest digital-bond sale.

The issuance boom has also helped cement the city’s global standing. Digital bonds issued in Hong Kong captured nearly 50% of the global market between 2025 and the first half of 2026, according to notes from Lee’s policy address last week. The government said it aims to use digital currencies for settlement and explore blockchain-based processes for dividend payment and redemption.

See also: Hong Kong Stock Exchange to discuss extended trading hours

The momentum is spreading across Asia, too. Earlier this month, Indian state-owned power financier REC Ltd issued five billion rupees (US$59 million or $67 million) of digital bonds due in May 2028.

title: RBI said to conduct at least US$10 bil FX swaps to drain cash — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 24): India’s central bank carried out currency swaps worth at least US$10 billion in recent weeks to reduce liquidity in the financial system, according to people familiar with the developments, as the authority seeks to curb inflation risks from surplus cash.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) conducted the so-called sell-buy swaps with lenders over the past two weeks, including deals with maturities ranging from one month to about six months, the people said, asking not to be named discussing private matters.

In such transactions, the RBI sells dollars to banks in exchange for rupees, agreeing to reverse the deal at a later date. By taking rupees from banks, the swaps drain rupee liquidity from the system. Rates on dollar-rupee contracts maturing in three months to six months have climbed this month, reflecting the central bank’s activity, the people said.

The RBI’s recent swaps are larger than similar steps that have been publicly announced over the past few years, largely reflecting the scale of the cash surplus that the central bank is currently tackling. Typically, the RBI carries out public swap auctions in tranches of around US$3 billon to US$5 billion.

A spokesperson for the central bank did not respond to an email seeking comment.

See also: South Korea starts trial run of 24-hour won settlement system

Lenders have been awash with cash after the RBI’s measures to attract foreign capital raked in more than US$140 billion, far exceeding official expectations. The inflows pushed surplus banking liquidity to a record 11 trillion rupees (US$115 billion) earlier this month, pushing down borrowing costs and worsening inflation risks from high oil prices.

“The RBI has been managing the liquidity build-up using bond sales and sell-buy swaps,” said Gaura Sen Gupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank Ltd. “Without these tools, the surplus would have peaked at 15.5 trillion rupees.”

The central bank may have carried out around US$10 billion to US$15 billion of sell-buy swaps maturing within the fiscal year ending March 31, she said.
